title: Mismatch to Calibration: Evolutionary and Developmental Considerations
abstract: Abstract Evolutionary mismatch theory proposes that traits adaptive in ancestral environments become maladaptive in modern contexts. The framing most often carried into psychological accounts has emphasized ancestral-modern discordance more than ongoing calibration. Standard clinical vocabulary can also make the problem appear to reside in the response itself rather than in the relation between calibrated expectations and present conditions. This paper reframes mismatch as a lag in calibration across three interacting currents. Phylogenetic inheritance provides species-typical architectures and biases shaped over evolutionary time. Ontogenetic development tunes those inherited potentials through individual experience across the lifespan. Cultural environments further structure the cues through which those systems are expressed, often on timescales far faster than either genetic change or individual development. Because these currents operate at different rates, temporary misalignment is inevitable even when all systems function correctly. Drawing on Bjorklund’s concept of evolved probabilistic cognitive mechanisms , this framework treats adaptations as emerging through continuous, bidirectional interaction across genetic, developmental, and cultural levels. Using anxiety and fear responses as illustrative examples, the paper demonstrates how ancient threat-detection systems continue adjusting to contemporary settings through partially dissociable processing pathways for phylogenetically primed versus ontogenetically acquired threats. This calibration perspective offers a more precise account of human functioning: anxiety and fear responses that have become chronic or rigid in present conditions may reflect defensive organization calibrated under prior conditions and carried forward into environments that no longer warrant the same thresholds of vigilance. Where evolutionary mismatch theory operates at the phylogenetic level, explaining how a discordance came about and why, the calibration framework operates at the ontogenetic level, asking whether a given mismatch in a given individual can change, and if so, how and when. The framework carries implications for intervention: therapeutic change can be understood as revising expectations forged under earlier conditions.
